 “We were asked to leave”: How F&B tenants are squeezing out a 32 Y/O S’pore toy shop
 Angelynn T. 
 16 Nov 2026 
 [sponsored-tag]
 Tom & Stefanie has gone from 10 outlets to 3 in 10 years 
 You’ve probably walked past a Tom & Stefanie store without giving it much thought. The name sounds like it could belong to an overseas chain, and Stefanie Chua, 22, the shop’s second-generation owner, says many Singaporeans assume it does.
 But it doesn’t. Her parents opened the kids’ clothing, toys and baby products shop in 1994, and it is entirely homegrown. Today, Stefanie, a Year 2 business student at SMU, is steering the business’s strategy.
 At its peak, the shop had 10 outlets. After its Hillion Mall store closed this year, three remain. But her plan isn’t to get back to 10. It’s to make the three that are left worth a trip for today’s shoppers.
 Growing up in the business 
 One of Tom & Stefanie’s old stores back in the early 2010s. Its founders picked “Tom” from Tom & Jerry because they wanted a name kids would recognise, and chose the “Stefanie” spelling because it felt unique./ Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 Stefanie’s parents opened Tom & Stefanie in 1994, when they were just 23. Her mother had worked as a merchandiser for Japanese kids’ products, while her father was a sales executive at a gift and stationery company. 
 Together, they spotted a gap: children’s products were mostly sold in department stores in town, far from where young families lived.
 So they bet on the heartlands, with quality products that were convenient, affordable and carefully curated. Stefanie likens the original concept to a mini Toys “R” Us, a one-stop department store with toys for all ages from global and local brands, plus clothes for toddlers.
 To open the first store under a Woodlands HDB block, her parents pooled a five-figure sum from family and their own savings. And within a year, a second neighbourhood outlet followed, and then the malls: White Sands, North Point and a 14,000 sq ft flagship at West Mall.
 (Left): Stefanie modelling for dresses sold at Tom & Stefanie; (Right): Stefanie’s younger brothers at the store./ Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 Stefanie spent weekends and school holidays in the stores, wrapping gifts at Christmas. She and her two younger brothers also worked as cashiers and served customers.
 But the experience didn’t make her want the job. “I actually felt a bit embarrassed about it last time,” she shared, recalling how she thought retail couldn’t compare in prestige to a corporate career.
 So she planned on a stable corporate path and took a gap year as an apprentice in sales and trading at JPMorgan.
 Then she realised she didn’t want a corporate life, and that she had skills that could help the family business. Outlets were closing one by one, and having seen how hard her parents had worked to build it, she decided to step in. In Nov 2025, in her first year at SMU, Stefanie joined the business to save it from shutting down.
 “Seeing something so central to my childhood and family slowly fade was heartbreaking,” she said in a previous interview with AsiaOne .
 She had to do everything by herself 
 By the time Stefanie joined the business, six of its 10 outlets had closed over the previous decade, including its West Mall flagship in 2023.
 To help drive business, Stefanie posted a TikTok video in Nov 2025 about the story behind the store and its struggles. A week later, it had passed 265,000 views, and her social media push has since drawn renewed interest from a new generation of customers.
 Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 But running a family business turned out to be nothing like corporate life, where everything runs on standard operating procedures. At Tom & Stefanie, the 22-year-old says, “you have to do everything by yourself,” from working out how GST works to charging suppliers, with no one guiding her.
 Her parents, the accountants and the admin staff are still on board, but she says the strategic direction is “mainly me.” Her parents are “still quite old school,” and it took “a lot” to convince them to even change up the space.
 Squeezed out by F&B tenants 
 Despite these efforts, Tom & Stefanie lost another outlet this year in Mar, its six-year-old Hillion Mall store.
 “We didn’t lose this store. We were asked to leave it. There’s a difference,” it wrote in an Instagram post announcing the closure. 
 Tom & Stefanie’s Hillion Mall outlet./ Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 Stefanie said renewal talks, which began in Jan, ended with the landlord proposing “significantly higher rental terms” than expected. She told MS News that the landlord planned to convert the space into an F&B outlet.
 Hillion Mall told Mothership that it regularly reviews its tenant mix and was refreshing Basement 1, where the brand’s store was located. It said it gave early notice and offered an alternative unit, which Tom & Stefanie declined. 
 However, Stefanie said that the offered unit was on the mall’s highest floor and would have “materially changed” how the store ran.
 Hillion Mall isn’t the first time Tom & Stefanie has been squeezed out. Stefanie says rent is the main reason the chain shrank, and F&B tenants are a big part of it.
 Most landlords prefer F&Bs because they can pay much more. We have been chased out of multiple malls actually because of F&Bs taking over.
 Stefanie Chua 
 She added that the brand had faced similar renewal problems at Tiong Bahru Plaza, Sun Plaza and City Square. One outlet’s rent even went up 30% on renewal, Stefanie said, though she didn’t specify which one. 
 Tom & Stefanie’s Sun Plaza outlet./ Image Credit: Michelle M. via Yelp 
 Leases typically run for three years, so businesses can expect an increase, but Stefanie calls that one “quite insane.” And with shoppers so price-conscious, she said the shop can’t pass the cost on.
 Tom & Stefanie is just one of many tenants Vulcan Post has spoken to, and its story echoes what we found at The Woodleigh Mall , where landlords can have financial reasons to hold out for higher-paying tenants instead of cutting rents.
 For now, Tom & Stefanie’s three remaining outlets are still within their current leases, so none is up for renewal, she shared.
 Making the stores worth a visit 
 Tom & Stefanie’s unique selling point is offering competitive pricing./ Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 Besides this, online competition is also putting pressure on the homegrown departmental store business, offering shoppers convenience and often cheaper prices.
 Tom & Stefanie keeps its prices low to attract customers too. In a Mediacorp programme, Stefanie pointed out that a car organiser at the store was S$44.90, cheaper than the S$57.12 found online.
 The store deliberately accepts lower margins and leans on long-term supplier relationships and direct links to factories, a strategy her parents have been running for more than 30 years.
 But low prices alone aren’t enough. With everything now a few taps away and delivered to the doorstep, Stefanie said, “you really have to give them a reason to even come down to the stores.”
 So she has been setting up small experiential booths inside the stores since around Apr this year, offering fidget clickers and DIY squishies, and earlier, DIY goodie bags. 
 Clickers designed and 3D-printed by Stefanie (left), alongside Singapore-themed clickers from Singaporean brand Heyo Makers (right)./ Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 Stefanie tests each idea for three to four weeks, then asks the staff whether it’s gaining traction. If it isn’t, it’s scrapped. Plenty of ideas haven’t made the cut.
 Over time, the booths have paid off. By her calculations, the items on them earn higher margins than the branded toys the shop sells as a retailer.
 The effect is most visible at Paya Lebar Quarter, she said, where a table with rolling pins for decorating slime draws shoppers who photograph and film it for social media. Many toys are also on open display, so customers can touch and try them before buying.
 Strong reception from these experiential DIY booths led to Confetti Club , a Tom & Stefanie service that hosts squishy-making sessions for birthday parties and company team bonding. Sessions start from S$16 per person for a minimum of 10 people, plus a one-time S$150 travel and set-up fee. It has recently collaborated with Butter Studio for a corporate team bonding session.
 Becoming the go-to store for parents in Singapore 
 A DIY squishy station at Tom & Stefanie./ Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 But making the change meant breaking from a routine that had stayed the same for 30 years.
 Stefanie’s parents see the store as a place to sell, not to experience. Because they pay per square foot, she said, they feel every inch should go to stocking more products. She disagrees, saying the business “needs to have an enjoyable experience for customers to even come in.”
 She also put the store online, but Shopee wasn’t the answer. 
 It made almost no sales, Stefanie said, since many of the brands the shop carries already sell on their own platforms. Instead, she is working on a revamped website featuring 100 bestselling toys, down from more than 3,000 products.
 Staff told her most customers come to buy gifts, so the shop is also leaning into that. The brand now has its own wrapping paper and paper bags. 
 Not everything is changing though. 
 Stefanie says two things from her parents’ approach are staying: affordability and trust. They keep prices low even where margins are slim, such as the shop’s dresses, and have turned down products over safety concerns, preferring to forgo the money.
 Image Credit: Tom & Stefanie 
 For now, Stefanie is happy that annual sales have picked up since she took over and has improved by double digits this year, something she calls “encouraging.”
 Her short-term goal is a better Christmas season for the business. In the longer term, she wants Tom & Stefanie to be the first shop parents think of when they’re stuck on what to buy a child for a birthday.
